summary: A 19.8 mm diameter silicon-nitride metasurface generates an 18,225-site optical tweezer array that traps 11,022 ± 167 $^{87}$Rb atoms with 60.5% filling fraction, reaching the tens-of-thousands-qubit scale for the first time across all platforms. The metasurface is positioned 1.5 cm outside the vacuum cell, eliminating the need for microscope objectives and achieving superior power efficiency (0.823 mW per tweezer, 12.2 W total diffraction power) compared to conventional SLM and AOD approaches.
motivation: Scaling beyond 6,100 atoms (the previous record from dual SLMs) requires overcoming fundamental bottlenecks in power utilization, diffraction efficiency, and working distance; conventional high-NA microscope objectives inherently limit addressable field-of-view and introduce attenuation, damage thresholds, and fabrication complexity.
method: A centimeter-scale metasurface with subwavelength nanostructure control was designed using blocked fast Fourier transforms to compensate for spherical aberrations through the Pyrex cell, fabricated via electron-beam lithography with thermal-drift correction and reactive-ion-etching optimization to maintain uniformity across the 19.8 mm diameter, and deployed 2.5 mm outside a standard cold-atom vacuum cell to achieve NA = 0.58 and Airy disk radius of 1.11 µm.
result: The system traps 11,000 atoms with a standard deviation of only 167 atoms over 100 iterations, achieves 13.2% power non-uniformity across the array, delivers a measured trap depth of 0.305 mK, and produces site-resolved loading probabilities peaking at 60%; finite-size percolation analysis reveals a critical loading fraction $p_c ≈ 0.59$ consistent with statistical mechanics predictions.
